analysis.one_liner: Lets student borrowers refinance federal and private student loans at zero percent interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate education committee on the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Department of Education refinance existing federal student loans with new loans that carry no interest at all, automatically for Direct Loan borrowers and by application for older federal loan types. It would also create a new federal loan that borrowers with private student loans could use to pay off their private lender and replace it with a zero-interest federal loan. The program would run from August 2022 through the end of 2025, and borrowers would keep their original repayment timelines so the benefit is purely the eliminated interest, not a longer payoff period.
analysis.who_benefits: People already carrying federal student loans — Direct, older FFEL, Perkins, and certain health-professions loans — who would stop accruing interest for the life of the loan, and people with private student loans, who could move their balances to a zero-interest federal loan. Because no interest would accrue, every dollar a borrower paid would go to principal, shortening payoff and cutting the total cost of the loan, often by thousands of dollars over the life of the debt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal and private student loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Education would automatically refinance Federal Direct Loans into zero-interest loans and notify each borrower, with no application required for Direct Loan holders.
Borrowers with older federal loans — FFEL, Perkins, and certain health profession and nursing loans — could apply to have them refinanced into zero-interest federal loans.
A new Federal Direct Refinanced Private Loan would let private student loan borrowers pay off their private lender with a zero-interest federal loan, after mandatory loan counseling.

Refinanced loans would not extend the repayment period, so borrowers would keep their original payoff schedule and gain the full benefit of the eliminated interest, and past payments would still count toward income-driven repayment and forgiveness programs.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government pays: it issues new loans with no interest, giving up all future interest income on the refinanced balances, and pays off private lenders in full for balances moved into the program. The bill directs the Education Department to set lender eligibility rules to preclude windfall profits, but the buyout of private loans at principal plus accrued interest would still be a large new federal outlay. Taxpayers as a whole bear that cost; it is uncapped in the bill and not tied to a specific funding source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via new federal lending

drawbacks.text: The program is temporary and closed: it covers loans first disbursed before January 2026, so future students and anyone taking loans after the window gets nothing, creating a sharp cutoff between otherwise similar borrowers.

The bill specifies no funding or budget offset; the Treasury would forgo interest on every refinanced federal loan and pay private lenders their full unpaid principal, accrued interest, and late charges, a substantial and uncapped cost.

The private-loan buyout requires paying private lenders off in full, and while the bill directs regulators to preclude windfall profits, only payments made after refinancing count toward forgiveness for borrowers who moved private loans into the program.

Borrowers with very low rates could end up worse off on the private-loan side if their existing rate was below what a zero-interest federal loan's sibling terms imply, and refinancing private loans into federal ones makes previously dischargeable private debt into federal debt that is much harder to discharge in bankruptcy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, eliminating interest is the single largest direct cost saver available short of cancellation, and the bill's design is careful: automatic refinancing, no extension of repayment terms, preserved credit toward forgiveness, and counseling before the private-loan switch. The honest cost is fiscal — an uncapped federal outlay to forgo interest and buy out private lenders — and the honest objection is the hard cutoff that leaves future students out. On its own terms it is a well-drafted, targeted benefit; whether the country should pay that price for that cohort is a genuine policy argument, not a drafting flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on May 26, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No senator from either party joined as a cosponsor.
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor consideration occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student borrowers who would have stopped paying interest keep paying it, and private student lenders keep collecting interest on their existing portfolios with no federal buyout. The committee and party leaders whose agenda the bill never reached avoided a vote on it entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student borrowers keep paying interest; private lenders keep it

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to the HELP Committee; recruited no cosponsors in the seven months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Patty Murray, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote in the roughly seven months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the record shows no motion to proceed, no floor debate, and no vote at any point.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support to be tested: a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote on which a party split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would pay private lenders off in full for every loan a borrower moves to the zero-interest federal program, a one-time windfall-free buyout, but it would permanently drain their interest-earning borrower base and subject them to new market-reporting requirements. Their standing business model — charging student borrowers interest year after year — runs directly against what the bill offers borrowers.

Refinanced loans remain federal loans serviced through the federal system, so the servicing industry keeps its role and volume, though zero-interest balances shrink the late fees and interest-driven revenue tied to servicing.
Treasury would forgo interest income on every refinanced loan and buy out private lenders in full, an uncapped cost; borrowers are the direct beneficiaries of that spending.
